items.followUp: What is the scientific name of humans, and which part is the genus name?

rubric.why: Shows that a scientific name consists of two parts.
rubric.description: States that binomial nomenclature gives each organism a two-part scientific name: genus and species.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying both parts.

rubric.why: Identifies the scientist who introduced the system.
rubric.description: Names Carolus Linnaeus as the person who introduced binomial nomenclature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct name.

modelAnswer: Binomial nomenclature is the system of naming each organism with two names: its genus name and species name.
It was introduced by Carolus Linnaeus.

items.followUp: Name the plastids that store starch and those that contain pigments.

rubric.why: Leucoplasts are colourless plastids that store food.
rubric.description: States that leucoplasts store food, such as starch, oils or proteins.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct storage function.

rubric.why: Chromoplast pigments give colour to plant parts.
rubric.description: States that chromoplasts contain pigments that give colour to flowers and fruits.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the pigment and colour function.

modelAnswer: Leucoplasts are colourless plastids that store food, such as starch, oils and proteins.
Chromoplasts contain pigments that give colour to flowers and fruits.

items.followUp: State one function of the Golgi apparatus and one function of mitochondria.

rubric.why: Ribosomes attached to rough ER are involved in protein synthesis.
rubric.description: States that rough endoplasmic reticulum has ribosomes and is involved in protein synthesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking rough ER/ribosomes with protein synthesis.

rubric.why: Smooth ER lacks ribosomes and performs other functions, including lipid synthesis and detoxification.
rubric.description: States a function of smooth endoplasmic reticulum, such as lipid synthesis or detoxification.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct smooth ER function.

modelAnswer: Rough endoplasmic reticulum has ribosomes on its surface and helps in protein synthesis.
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum has no ribosomes and is involved in lipid synthesis and detoxification.

items.followUp: What is a cell plate, and how does it form during plant-cell division?

rubric.why: Locates the phragmoplast in the context of plant-cell division.
rubric.description: Identifies the phragmoplast as a structure formed during plant-cell cytokinesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct context.

rubric.why: The phragmoplast helps form the cell plate between daughter cells.
rubric.description: States that the phragmoplast guides or helps in cell-plate formation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for its role in cell-plate formation.

modelAnswer: The phragmoplast is a structure formed between the daughter nuclei during cytokinesis in plant cells.
It guides the formation of the cell plate, which develops into the new cell wall between the daughter cells.

items.followUp: During which stage of meiosis do homologous chromosomes pair, and what is this pairing called?

rubric.description: States that synapsis is the pairing of homologous chromosomes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the chromosomes that pair.

rubric.why: Places synapsis in the correct stage of meiosis.
rubric.description: States that synapsis occurs during prophase I, specifically the zygotene stage.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct stage.

modelAnswer: Synapsis is the pairing of homologous chromosomes during prophase I of meiosis.
It takes place during the zygotene stage.

items.followUp: How does an enzyme's active site help a substrate undergo a reaction?

rubric.why: The active site binds the substrate.
rubric.description: States that the active site provides a place for the substrate to bind.

rubric.why: The active site enables or facilitates the enzyme-catalysed reaction.
rubric.description: States that the active site facilitates catalysis, such as by speeding the reaction or lowering activation energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct catalytic role.

modelAnswer: The active site binds the specific substrate.
It facilitates the reaction by catalysing it, lowering the activation energy and increasing the reaction rate.

items.followUp: What is meant by the lock-and-key model of enzyme action?

rubric.why: Enzyme specificity means an enzyme acts on a particular substrate or type of reaction.
rubric.description: States that an enzyme acts on a specific substrate or type of reaction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the selective action.

rubric.why: Specificity is explained by the fit between the substrate and the active site.
rubric.description: Explains that specificity is due to the substrate fitting the enzyme's active site.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for relating specificity to the active-site fit.

modelAnswer: Specificity of an enzyme is its ability to act on a particular substrate or catalyse a particular reaction.
This is because only a suitable substrate fits the enzyme's active site.

items.followUp: How is energy stored in ATP and released for cellular activities?

rubric.why: ATP stores readily available chemical energy for cell activities.
rubric.description: States that ATP stores or carries usable chemical energy in the cell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the energy-storage or energy-carrier role.

rubric.why: Energy is released when ATP loses its terminal phosphate group.
rubric.description: Explains that ATP releases energy when its terminal phosphate bond is broken, forming ADP and phosphate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the phosphate-bond breakdown explanation.

modelAnswer: ATP is called the energy currency of the cell because it stores and transfers readily available chemical energy for cellular activities.
When its terminal phosphate bond is broken, ATP forms ADP and phosphate and releases energy.
